classification_signals: The abstract states, 'This paper attempts to provide a new way of looking at the human-environment relationship'.
The introduction states, 'The purpose of this paper is to propose a framework for conceptualizing what 'poorly designed means...'.
The conclusion explicitly states, 'It should be emphasized that this paper is a theoretical analysis, not an empirical demonstration.' (p. 59).
The 'Empirical Studies' section reviews existing literature to support theoretical claims, rather than presenting new data.
title: MENTAL FATIGUE AND THE DESIGNED ENVIRONMENT

findings.quote: directed attention not only requires effort but can also become fatigued.
mental fatigue is costly in terms of human effectiveness.
Mental fatigue expresses itself not only. in terms of being ineffectual, but also in irritability and discomfort as well.

findings.antecedent: struggling to function in poorly designed environments
findings.quote: at least some of the consequences of struggling to function in poorly designed environments can appropri-ately be attributed to mental fatigue.
Mental fatigue is a state of discomfort and reduced effectiveness that usually follows intense mental effort...

findings.antecedent: sleep or larger recovery efforts (e.g., vacation)
findings.quote: Modest levels of mental fatigue may be relieved by sleep; more substantial deficits are likely to require correspondingly larger recovery efforts, such as taking a vacation.
growing evidence pointing to the close relationship between mental fatigue and a decline in the capacity to direct attention.

findings.antecedent: struggling to maintain focus despite distraction
findings.quote: when one struggles to maintain focus despite distraction the capacity to direct one's attention gradually declines.

findings.antecedent: further demands on an already fatigued capacity (to direct attention)
findings.quote: Further demands on an already fatigued capacity make recovery even more difficult.

findings.consequent: mental fatigue (via extensive directed attention use)
findings.quote: Environments that are boring or distracting or unsafe require extensive use of directed attention, leading ultimately to mental fatigue.
Mental fatigue is a cumulative state.
Environments of different scales, and that are unsatisfactory in many different ways, can all contribute to an individual's mental fatigue.

findings.antecedent: open plan office, traffic, confusing car controls
findings.quote: trying to work in an open plan office, being stuck in traffic on the way home to work, and having difficulty figuring out the meaning of the controls of one's new car can all contribute to an individual's mental fatigue.
People have a substantial capacity to incur a deficit and pay later.
When in such a fatigued state, an individual is likely to be impatient, irritable, and prone to making errors.
Being in such a state is unlikely to contribute to either effective functioning or to an enhanced quality of life.
Designing to avoid mental fatigue could thus help define what we mean by 'good design.'
involuntary attention... is automatic and effortless but not under the control of the perceiver.
big, bright and noisy stimuli readily catch one's attention.
While such patterns can make one's task easier when they are task relevant...

findings.antecedent: big, bright, noisy stimuli (not task relevant)
findings.quote: ...they can also serve as powerful distractors when they are not.

findings.antecedent: extensive use of central inhibitory capacity (for directed attention)
findings.quote: It is this central inhibitory capacity which is assuemd to be susceptible to fatigue following extensive use.

findings.antecedent: competing information sources (e.g., confusing environment, internal worries)
findings.quote: The first (and most straightforward) involves dealing with competing information sources.
A second function of dinected attention involves the making and carrying out of plans.

findings.antecedent: social situations (e.g., listening to others, inhibiting disruptive behavior)
findings.quote: A third function is social in nature.
As fatigue increases, the capacity to direct attention declines.
Attention becomes not only more difficult and effortful, but less effective as well.

findings.consequent: management of conflict, distractibility, errors, planning, social relations (anger, violence)
findings.quote: The consequences of fatigue are the failures of the very func-tions discussed above.
Accident reports that place the blame on 'human error' may be referring to consequences of mental fatigue.

findings.consequent: feeling less attentive, tired, irritable, generalized mental fatigue
findings.quote: Following a vigilance task people not only feel less attentive, but also tired and irritable (Warm & Dember, 1986), suggesting a state of generalized mental fatigue.

findings.consequent: inability to carry out tasks demanding directed attention (unfamiliar, dull, prolonged, low complexity)
findings.quote: After prolonged sleep deprivation, people are unable to carry out tasks that are unfamiliar, dull, prolonged or low in complexity (Kleitman, 1963; Wilkinson, 1965), just the sort of situations that would demand directed attention.

findings.consequent: willingness to help someone in need
findings.quote: Following such an experience individuals are less likely to be willing to help someone in need (Sherrod & Downs, 1974; Cohen & Spacapan, 1978).

findings.antecedent: attention-demanding tasks under high distraction (fatigued attentional capacity)
findings.consequent: aggression, tolerance of frustration, sensitivity to socially important cues
findings.quote: They are also more aggressive (Donnerstein & Wilson, 1976), less tolerant of frustration (Cohen & Spacapan, 1978), and less sensitive to socially important cues (Cohen & Lezak, 1977).
Here again a fatigued attentional capacity is associated with what appears to be a pervasive decline in inhibitory control.
Opportunities for recovery are provided by situations where directed attention is allowed to rest. We have come to call environments which make this possible 'restorative environments.'
Wilderness, at least for some people, turns out to be a particularly effective restora-tive environment (Kaplan & Talbot, 1983; Talbot & Kaplan, 1986)
Briefer encounters with these more modest forms of nature can also contribute to recovery.

findings.consequent: recovery of directed attention (via involuntary attention/fascination)
findings.quote: Gardening, for example, brings with it a strong fascination (in other words, involuntary attention) thus permitting the recovery of directed attention (R. Kaplan, 1973).
Such possibilities of 'micro-restorative experiences' are particularly salient to creating designed environments tha: reduce the burden of mental fatigue.

findings.antecedent: environment with different content (diversity, natural materials)
findings.quote: It is helpful to have content that is different from the concerns that normally occupy the mind. Diversity can play an important role here... Natural materials provide one way to change the content.

findings.antecedent: environmental fascination (e.g., urban parks, moving water, people watching)
findings.quote: The fascination that is built into the situation offers an important basis for resting directed attention.

findings.antecedent: environmental coherence (parts related, manageable for mind)
findings.quote: Coherence is necessary for the result to be experienced as a whole rather than many competing stimuli.

findings.antecedent: environmental compatibility (with individual goals/inclinations, allowing expression of making sense/learning)
findings.quote: There must be compatibility with an individual's goals and inclinations.

findings.antecedent: environmental choice (allowing selection of appropriate portions)
findings.quote: Given choices invidividuals have the possibility of selecting appropriate portions or aspects of the enviornment appropriate to their goals at that point in time.

findings.antecedent: gardens, quality of view out window
findings.quote: Gardens have been repeatedly shown to have powerful restorative effects, and even the quality of the view out the window makes an important contribution (R. Kaplan, 1983).

findings.antecedent: environments (necessitating considerable directed attention use, e.g., for wayfinding)
findings.quote: Environments vary widely in their attentional demands. Some necessitate considerable use of directed attention to carry out such basic activities as wayfinding.
At the other extreme, some environments combine the important and useful to the degree that directed attention can rest much of the time.
Confusion... problems as illegibility and the confusion that results are by no means restricted to the city scale.
Confusion is costly; fortunately it can often be prevented by effective design.

findings.consequent: mental fatigue (via heavy burden on directed attention)
findings.quote: Distraction is a second property of the environment that takes its toll in terms of mental fatigue.
Through the use of stimuli designed to be fascinating, advertisers capture the unwitting attention of passersby.

findings.antecedent: environmental incompatibility (with purposes/inclinations) leading to helplessness (inability to change)
findings.quote: Helplessness is a costly state of mind, leading to rapid mental fatigue.
participation in decisions about an environment is not only likely to improve the environment, but also the mental state of those who have the opportunity to participate.

findings.antecedent: environmental familiarity (via reduction in unnecessary change)
findings.quote: reduction in the rate of unnecessary change... Effectiveness in an environment, as well as the reduction in the directed attention necessary to function in it, requires familiarity.

limitations: This paper is a theoretical analysis, not an empirical demonstration.
Directed attention is a vital element in many valued activities, and as such, mental fatigue will always be endemic.
It is impossible to anticipate all possible human goals in the design process, which impacts environmental compatibility.
minimum_safe_summary: This paper proposes a conceptual framework linking mental fatigue to the design of the environment. It argues that poorly designed environments, characterized by high attentional demands, distraction, confusion, and lack of compatibility, contribute to mental fatigue. Mental fatigue, in turn, reduces human effectiveness, increases irritability, and impairs social functioning. The paper suggests two strategies for managing mental fatigue: recovery through restorative environments (e.g., nature, fascination, coherence, compatibility, choice) and prevention through effective design that minimizes confusion, distraction, helplessness, and unnecessary change. A key limitation is that this is a theoretical analysis, not an empirical demonstration, and mental fatigue is acknowledged as an endemic aspect of valued human activities.
